## Introduction

The {coresynth} package is an R package I developed to implement methods related to the synthetic control method easily and quickly, including the Synthetic Control Method (SCM), Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDID), Generalized Synthetic Control (GSC), and Matrix Completion (MC). While [the previous post](../coresynth_scm/index.qmd) covered the basic synthetic control method, this post focuses on **Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDID)**, walking step-by-step from an overview of the method to model estimation, visualization, and inference procedures using coresynth.

## What is Synthetic Difference-in-Differences?

Proposed by @arkhangelsky_synthetic_2021 in the *American Economic Review*, Synthetic Difference-in-Differences is an important method in causal inference. SDID combines two of the most widely used empirical methodologies in econometrics: **Difference-in-Differences (DID)** and the **Synthetic Control Method (SCM)** [@abadie_synthetic_2010].

Traditional DID relies on the **parallel trends assumption**, positing that in the absence of treatment, the average outcomes of the treated and control units would have moved in parallel over time. In practice, this assumption often fails when treated and untreated units differ substantially in their observable and unobservable characteristics. Standard DID also assigns uniform weights to all control units and all pre-treatment periods, regardless of how relevant they are for predicting the treated trajectory.

On the other hand, SCM constructs a data-driven weighted average of control units (unit weights $\omega_i$) to reproduce the treated unit's pre-treatment outcome levels. However, standard SCM does not incorporate an intercept shift (fixed effects) and restricts weights to the simplex ($\sum \omega_i = 1, \omega_i \ge 0$). As a result, when the treated unit lies outside the convex hull of the donor pool (for example, when the treated unit has a consistently higher baseline level than any donor), SCM cannot extrapolate, which can cause poor pre-treatment fit and bias.

SDID synthesizes the core strengths of both worlds by introducing three complementary mechanisms:

1. **Unit weights ($\hat\omega_i$)**: Control units are reweighted so that their weighted average moves in parallel with the treated unit before the intervention (matching up to a constant intercept $\omega_0$), relaxing the traditional DID requirement that all controls be parallel on average. A ridge penalty spreads the weight across many donors rather than a few.
2. **Time weights ($\hat\lambda_t$)**: Pre-treatment periods are reweighted so that the $\hat\lambda$-weighted pre-treatment average of the control units predicts their post-treatment average (again up to a constant $\lambda_0$). In practice, this puts most of the weight on the pre-treatment periods that most resemble the post-treatment period, which are often the most recent ones.
3. **Double differencing (Intercept shift)**: Like DID, SDID incorporates unit and time fixed effects, absorbing permanent level differences between the treated unit and the donor pool.

Mathematically, the SDID treatment effect for a single treated unit is expressed as:

$$\hat{\tau}^{\text{sdid}} = \left( \bar{Y}_{\text{post}}^{\text{tr}} - \sum_{t=1}^{T_{\text{pre}}} \hat{\lambda}_t Y_{1t} \right) - \sum_{i \in \text{control}} \hat{\omega}_i \left( \bar{Y}_{\text{post}, i} - \sum_{t=1}^{T_{\text{pre}}} \hat{\lambda}_t Y_{it} \right)$$

where $\bar{Y}_{\text{post}}^{\text{tr}}$ is the post-treatment average of the treated unit, $Y_{1t}$ is the treated unit's outcome at pre-treatment time $t$, and $\bar{Y}_{\text{post}, i}$ is the post-treatment average of control unit $i$. With several treated units adopting at the same time, the treated series is replaced by their cross-sectional average. The intercepts $\omega_0$ and $\lambda_0$ cancel out in this double difference, so they do not appear in the formula.

## Why Use {coresynth} for SDID?

While {synthdid} is widely considered the standard R package for SDID, empirical causal inference frequently requires repeated computations: calculating standard errors via bootstrap, running leave-one-out placebo tests across dozens of donors, conducting sensitivity analyses, or testing multiple treatment specifications.

The {coresynth} package is designed and implemented in C++ via `RcppArmadillo` to enable fast analysis without sacrificing mathematical precision:

- **⚡ Fast Factor-Form Solvers**: SDID unit and time weights are solved by an accelerated projected-gradient method (FISTA) on the simplex. Since coresynth 1.0.1, the unit weights are solved directly in factor form rather than forming and decomposing the dense $N_{\text{co}} \times N_{\text{co}}$ donor Gram matrix, which made the placebo, jackknife, and bootstrap routines of `sdid_inference()` **about 6× faster** on a 300-donor panel.
- **🧩 Unified Interface**: Run SDID alongside SCM, Generalized Synthetic Control (GSC), Matrix Completion (MC), Time-Aware Synthetic Control (TASC), and Synthetic Interventions (SI) through the exact same `scm_fit()` formula syntax.
- **📊 Inference**: Native support for placebo permutation tests, unit bootstrap, jackknife, global jackknife (for staggered designs), conformal inference, and dynamic event studies (available in development version).
- **📈 Diagnostics**: Unified `plot()` methods with level-alignment (`align = TRUE`), donor path overlays (`show_donors`), and dual-panel weight visualizations.

## Setup & Installation

You can install the released version of coresynth from CRAN, or grab the latest development version directly from GitHub:

```r
# Install released version from CRAN
pak::pak("coresynth")

# Or install development version from GitHub
pak::pak("yo5uke/coresynth")
```

Next, let's load coresynth into your R session alongside {tidyverse}. For benchmark comparison, we also load {synthdid}.

```{r}
library(coresynth)
library(synthdid)
library(tidyverse)
```

## Data: California Proposition 99

To compare our results with [@arkhangelsky_synthetic_2021], we use the `smoking` dataset from the {tidysynth} package. This panel tracks per-capita cigarette sales across 39 US states from 1970 to 2000. California passed Proposition 99 in November 1988, taking effect in 1989.

```{r}
data("smoking", package = "tidysynth")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-smoking
#| tbl-cap: "Overview of the smoking panel dataset"
gt::gt(head(smoking, 5))
```

### Preparing the Binary Treatment Indicator

As in all coresynth estimators, `scm_fit()` requires a binary treatment column that equals `1` for the treated unit in the post-treatment period, and `0` otherwise:

```{r}
smoking <- smoking |>
  mutate(
    treated = if_else(state == "California" & year >= 1989, 1L, 0L)
  )
```

Because California enacted the policy starting in 1989, `treated` is `1` exclusively for California for years 1989 through 2000.

## Estimation with `scm_fit()`

In coresynth, you invoke SDID simply by setting `method = "sdid"`:

```r
core_sdid <- scm_fit(
  cigsale ~ treated | state + year,
  data = smoking,
  method = "sdid"
)
```

The model formula is specified in the form `outcome ~ treated | unit + time`.

### Speed Benchmark: {coresynth} vs. {synthdid}

We benchmark coresynth's execution speed against {synthdid} for the full routine of estimation followed by placebo inference:^[The two placebo routines do not run the same number of refits. With a single treated unit, coresynth assigns the placebo to each of the 38 control states in turn (the exhaustive placebo distribution), whereas `synthdid::synthdid_se(method = "placebo")` draws 200 random placebo assignments by default (`replications = 200`). Part of the gap therefore comes from the number of refits rather than from the speed of each one.]

:::{.panel-tabset}
## {coresynth}

Here we run `scm_fit()` and immediately calculate the full placebo distribution via `sdid_inference()`:

```r
core_sdid <- scm_fit(
  cigsale ~ treated | state + year,
  data = smoking,
  method = "sdid"
)
core_placebo <- sdid_inference(core_sdid, method = "placebo")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
tictoc::tic()
core_sdid <- scm_fit(
  cigsale ~ treated | state + year,
  data = smoking,
  method = "sdid"
)
core_placebo <- sdid_inference(core_sdid, method = "placebo")
time_coresynth_res <- tictoc::toc()
time_coresynth <- sprintf(
  "%.2f",
  unname(time_coresynth_res$toc - time_coresynth_res$tic)
)
```

## {synthdid}

For comparison, here is the equivalent specification implemented in {synthdid} (note that `synthdid::panel.matrices()` requires a base `data.frame` rather than a `tibble` so that column subsetting returns a vector):

```r
setup <- synthdid::panel.matrices(
  smoking |>
    transmute(
      unit = state,
      time = year,
      y = cigsale,
      treated = treated
    ) |>
    as.data.frame()
)
sdid_est <- synthdid::synthdid_estimate(setup$Y, setup$N0, setup$T0)
sdid_se_plac <- synthdid::synthdid_se(sdid_est, method = "placebo")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
tictoc::tic()
setup <- synthdid::panel.matrices(
  smoking |>
    transmute(
      unit = state,
      time = year,
      y = cigsale,
      treated = treated
    ) |>
    as.data.frame()
)
sdid_est <- synthdid::synthdid_estimate(setup$Y, setup$N0, setup$T0)
sdid_se_plac <- synthdid::synthdid_se(sdid_est, method = "placebo")
time_synthdid_res <- tictoc::toc()
time_synthdid <- sprintf(
  "%.2f",
  unname(time_synthdid_res$toc - time_synthdid_res$tic)
)
speedup <- sprintf(
  "%.1f",
  as.numeric(time_synthdid) / as.numeric(time_coresynth)
)
```
:::

In this comparison, coresynth finishes in **`r time_coresynth` seconds**, whereas synthdid takes **`r time_synthdid` seconds**—a **`r speedup`× speedup**.

When running extensive sensitivity analyses, computing bootstrap standard errors, or testing multiple candidate donor pools, waiting for slow estimations quickly adds up. This efficiency gain was a core motivation behind developing coresynth.

### Inspecting the Model Summary

Calling `summary()` on a fitted SDID model prints the essential estimation metrics, including the pre/post period lengths, the estimated Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT), and the active donor unit weights:

```{r}
summary(core_sdid)
```

The estimated ATT indicates that Proposition 99 reduced California's cigarette consumption by approximately **15.6 packs per capita per year**, reproducing the SDID estimate of @arkhangelsky_synthetic_2021. Notice how this compares with the standard SCM ($\approx -19.6$ packs) and standard DID ($\approx -27.3$ packs) estimates they report for the same data: SDID accommodates level shifts while matching pre-treatment trends.

## Visualizing Trends, Level Alignment, and Weights

Visualizing results is important for credible causal inference. In SDID, counterfactual visualization requires extra care because the estimator incorporates an intercept shift and time weights.

### Raw Trajectory vs. Level-Aligned Plot (`align = TRUE`)

In standard SCM, the synthetic control directly matches the treated unit's pre-treatment level. In SDID, however, units match trends up to a free intercept shift. Consequently, a raw trajectory plot (`align = FALSE`, default) displays the synthetic series at its unadjusted level.

By specifying `align = TRUE`, coresynth offsets the synthetic series by the $\hat\lambda$-weighted pre-period gap. Under this alignment, the average post-treatment gap between the two lines equals the SDID treatment effect ($\hat\tau^{\text{sdid}}$) **exactly**:

:::{.panel-tabset}
## Level-Aligned Trend (`align = TRUE`)

```{r}
plot(core_sdid, type = "trend", align = TRUE)
```

The synthetic California series is vertically shifted so that the pre-treatment time-weighted baseline matches California, making the post-1988 divergence immediately interpretable as the causal effect.

## Raw Trend (`align = FALSE`)

```{r}
plot(core_sdid, type = "trend", align = FALSE)
```

The raw plot illustrates the actual unadjusted levels of the synthetic composite compared to California, highlighting the presence of a baseline level difference that SDID effectively absorbs.
:::

### Gap Plot

The gap plot (`type = "gap"`) plots the estimated treatment effect over time:

```{r}
plot(core_sdid, type = "gap", align = TRUE)
```

With `align = TRUE`, the pre-treatment gap fluctuates closely around zero (its $\hat\lambda$-weighted average is zero by construction), and the post-treatment line confirms the steady decrease in cigarette sales following the policy adoption.

### Inspecting Unit and Time Weights

A key feature of SDID is that it solves for both unit weights ($\hat\omega_i$) and pre-treatment time weights ($\hat\lambda_t$). Calling `plot(..., type = "weights")` on an SDID object generates a two-panel chart displaying both weight vectors:

```{r}
plot(core_sdid, type = "weights")
```

The top panel illustrates which donor states carry positive weight in constructing the synthetic counterfactual. Unlike the sparse SCM weights in [the previous post](../coresynth_scm/index.qmd), the ridge penalty spreads the SDID weights over 27 of the 38 donor states, with Nevada, New Hampshire, and Connecticut receiving the largest shares. The bottom panel displays the time weights $\hat\lambda_t$: all of the weight falls on the last three pre-treatment years (1986–1988), the periods that best predict the post-treatment level of the control states.

### Overlaying Donor Trajectories (`show_donors`)

To assess whether the synthetic control is interpolating plausibly among donor units, you can pass `show_donors = N` to draw the raw trajectories of the top $N$ donor states as thin background lines:

```{r}
plot(core_sdid, type = "trend", align = TRUE, show_donors = 5)
```

### Customizing Plots with ggplot2

Because all coresynth plots are standard `ggplot2` objects, you can easily customize styling, labels, colors, and line types using native ggplot2 grammar. For details on all arguments supported in `plot()`, see `?plot.coresynth`.

```{r}
plot(
  core_sdid,
  type = "trend",
  align = TRUE,
  colors = c(treated = "darkblue", synthetic = "firebrick"),
  labels = c(
    treated = "California (Observed)",
    synthetic = "SDID Counterfactual"
  ),
  linetypes = c(treated = "solid", synthetic = "dashed"),
  vline = list(color = "black", linetype = "dotted"),
  vline_offset = -1
) +
  labs(
    title = "Cigarette Sales in California vs. Synthetic DID Counterfactual",
    subtitle = "Proposition 99 Tobacco Control Program (1988)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Packs per Capita"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Statistical Inference with `sdid_inference()`

Quantifying statistical uncertainty is essential for credible causal evaluation. While SCM relied almost exclusively on permutation placebo tests [@abadie_synthetic_2010], SDID provides a framework with multiple inference methods [@arkhangelsky_synthetic_2021; @clarke_synthetic_2024].

In coresynth, statistical inference is unified under `sdid_inference()`. The function provides four primary inferential methods:

```r
sdid_inference(
  fit,
  method      = c("placebo", "bootstrap", "jackknife", "jackknife_global"),
  n_boot      = 200L,
  level       = 0.95,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less"),
  seed        = NULL
)
```

### Choosing the Right Inference Method

The appropriate choice of inference method depends primarily on the design of your study and the questions being asked:

- **Single Treated Unit ($N_{\text{tr}} = 1$)**: When only one unit is treated (as in our California study), no resampling of units can vary the treated unit's own idiosyncratic shocks. The bootstrap and the jackknife therefore stop with an error, and you should **use `method = "placebo"`**, which learns the noise level from the control units, or **Conformal Inference** (`conformal_inference()`).
- **Several Treated Units ($N_{\text{tr}} \ge 2$)**: The bootstrap (`method = "bootstrap"`, Algorithm 2) resamples treated and control units alike and re-runs the whole estimator, and the jackknife (`method = "jackknife"`, Algorithm 3) drops one unit at a time, treated or control, with the fitted weights held fixed. The placebo remains available as long as there are more control units than treated ones.
- **Staggered Adoption**: For roll-out designs where units adopt treatment at different times, the bootstrap rebuilds the adoption cohorts from the treated units drawn. The per-cohort `method = "jackknife"` needs at least two treated units in every cohort and combines the cohort variances by the delta method, ignoring the covariance that shared donors induce between cohorts; `method = "jackknife_global"` keeps that covariance by dropping each unit from the whole panel at once.
- **Distribution-Free Assumption**: For finite-sample validity without parametric noise assumptions, use **Conformal Inference** via `conformal_inference()` (sharp fits only).

### 1. Placebo Permutation Inference (`method = "placebo"`)

For California Proposition 99, where $N_{\text{tr}} = 1$, we employ the in-space placebo permutation procedure (Algorithm 4 of @arkhangelsky_synthetic_2021 and @clarke_synthetic_2024). California is set aside, and each of the 38 control states in turn is treated as if it had adopted the policy in 1989. For every placebo assignment, the whole SDID estimator, including $\hat\omega$, $\hat\lambda$, and the penalty, is re-estimated on the control states alone, yielding the placebo distribution $\{\hat\tau^{(b)}\}_{b=1}^{B}$:

```{r}
inf_placebo <- sdid_inference(core_sdid, method = "placebo")
inf_placebo
```

`inf_placebo$p_value` reports the two-sided permutation $p$-value, $\left(1 + \#\{b : |\hat\tau^{(b)}| \ge |\hat\tau|\}\right) / (B + 1)$, where $B = 38$ here. Additionally, `sdid_inference()` calculates the standard error as the standard deviation of the placebo distribution, $\widehat{\text{se}} = \sqrt{B^{-1} \sum_b (\hat\tau^{(b)} - \bar\tau)^2}$, alongside a normal-approximation confidence interval $\hat\tau \pm z_{1-\alpha/2} \, \widehat{\text{se}}$ (`ci_lower` and `ci_upper`).

When several units are treated, `n_boot` random sets of $N_{\text{tr}}$ control units receive the placebo instead (reproducible through `seed`), and on a staggered fit they take over the treated units' adoption dates. Either way, the placebo needs more control units than treated ones.

Notice that because the placebo standard error assumes the treated unit's noise variance is comparable to that of the donor units, it should be interpreted thoughtfully when donor pools are modest in size.

### 2. Unit Bootstrap (`method = "bootstrap"`)

In coresynth, `method = "bootstrap"` follows Algorithm 2 of @arkhangelsky_synthetic_2021 and @clarke_synthetic_2024. Each replicate draws $N$ units with replacement from the whole panel, **treated and control units alike**, and redraws any sample that contains no treated unit or no control unit. The whole estimator is then run again on the drawn panel: the covariate adjustment (if any), the noise level $\hat\sigma$ and penalty $\zeta$, and both sets of weights $\hat\omega$ and $\hat\lambda$. A unit drawn twice enters as two separate units.

Because the treated units are resampled too, the bootstrap requires **at least two treated units**. With a single treated unit, its own noise would never vary across replicates and the interval would be far too narrow, so `sdid_inference()` stops and points you to `method = "placebo"`. To illustrate how multi-unit inference operates in coresynth, let's generate a synthetic panel with 4 treated units and 20 control units:

```{r}
set.seed(42)
multi_panel <- expand.grid(unit = 1:24, year = 1990:2010)
multi_panel$treated <- as.integer(
  multi_panel$unit <= 4 & multi_panel$year >= 2002
)
multi_panel$y <- multi_panel$unit *
  1.5 +
  0.8 * (multi_panel$year - 1990) +
  rnorm(nrow(multi_panel), sd = 0.5) -
  2.5 * multi_panel$treated

fit_multi <- scm_fit(
  y ~ treated | unit + year,
  data = multi_panel,
  method = "sdid"
)
```

Now we execute the bootstrap with `n_boot = 200`:

```{r}
inf_boot <- sdid_inference(
  fit_multi,
  method = "bootstrap",
  n_boot = 200,
  seed = 123
)
inf_boot$se
inf_boot$p_value
c(inf_boot$ci_lower, inf_boot$ci_upper)
```

The standard error is the standard deviation of the bootstrap estimates, the confidence interval is the percentile interval of those estimates, and the $p$-value is the normal approximation based on $\hat\tau / \widehat{\text{se}}$.

### 3. Jackknife Variance Estimation (`method = "jackknife"`)

The jackknife follows Algorithm 3 of @arkhangelsky_synthetic_2021 and @clarke_synthetic_2024. It drops one unit at a time, **treated or control**, and recomputes the weighted difference-in-differences with the fitted weights held fixed: $\hat\lambda$ is kept as is, and $\hat\omega$ is renormalized over the remaining donors. The variance is $\widehat{V} = \frac{n-1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} (\hat\tau^{(-j)} - \bar\tau)^2$ over the $n$ leave-one-out estimates, and the confidence interval and $p$-value use the normal approximation. Like the bootstrap, it needs at least two treated units. Because no weights are re-optimized, it runs almost instantaneously:

```{r}
inf_jack <- sdid_inference(fit_multi, method = "jackknife")
inf_jack$se
inf_jack$p_value
```

For staggered adoption panels, `method = "jackknife_global"` drops each unit from the entire multi-cohort panel simultaneously, correctly preserving the covariance between cohorts.

### 4. Conformal Inference (`conformal_inference()`)

If you prefer hypothesis tests with finite-sample guarantees that avoid asymptotic approximations, coresynth provides Conformal Inference based on @chernozhukov_exact_2021. Under the null hypothesis $H_0: \tau = \tau_0$, it subtracts $\tau_0$ from the treated unit's post-treatment outcomes, re-estimates the counterfactual on all $T$ periods, and computes a moving-block (cyclic) permutation $p$-value from the residuals. The test is exact when the residuals are exchangeable over time and approximately valid under weak dependence. The confidence interval collects the values of $\tau_0$ that are not rejected:

```{r}
conf_res <- conformal_inference(core_sdid, level = 0.95)
conf_res$p_value
c(conf_res$ci_lower, conf_res$ci_upper)
```

The $p$-value at $\tau_0 = 0$ is `r round(conf_res$p_value, 3)`, so conformal inference does not reject the null of no effect for California, and the interval is very wide. With $T = 31$ periods there are only 31 cyclic permutations, so the $p$-value is a multiple of $1/31$, and a candidate $\tau_0$ is rejected at the 5% level only if its post-treatment residuals are the most extreme of all 31 blocks.

## Dynamic Effects & Event Studies: `sdid_event_study()`

> [!NOTE]
> `sdid_event_study()` is currently available only in the development version of coresynth (`pak::pak("yo5uke/coresynth")`).

Researchers often want to inspect dynamic treatment trajectories—confirming that pre-treatment coefficients are indistinguishable from zero (pre-trend check) while tracing out how effects unfold post-intervention.

coresynth provides the dedicated `sdid_event_study()` function for this purpose (sharp fits only). It computes period-by-period treatment effects aligned on the $\hat\lambda$-weighted pre-treatment baseline,

$$\hat\delta_t = \left(\bar{Y}^{\text{tr}}_t - \sum_{i} \hat\omega_i Y_{it}\right) - \sum_{s=1}^{T_{\text{pre}}} \hat\lambda_s \left(\bar{Y}^{\text{tr}}_s - \sum_{i} \hat\omega_i Y_{is}\right),$$

so the post-treatment average of the period-specific coefficients equals the aggregate SDID ATT (`fit$estimate`) **exactly**. Standard errors come from the same unit bootstrap as `sdid_inference(method = "bootstrap")`, which resamples treated and control units and re-estimates the weights on every draw, and both normal-approximation and percentile intervals are reported:

```{r}
es_res <- sdid_event_study(
  fit_multi,
  n_boot = 100,
  seed = 42
)
es_res
```

### Visualizing the Event Study

You can plot the event-study trajectory directly using the S3 `plot()` method:

```{r}
plot(es_res)
```

The resulting figure displays period-specific point estimates accompanied by confidence interval bands. The pre-treatment periods center closely around zero, while the post-treatment drop vividly illustrates the causal effect over time. Keep in mind that the pre-treatment coefficients are constrained by the weights themselves (their $\hat\lambda$-weighted average is zero by construction), so they serve as a visual check rather than a formal pre-trend test.

### Cluster Bootstrap Support

If units belong to geographical clusters (such as districts within states or prefectures), you can pass `cluster = "cluster_var"` and `data = panel_df` to `sdid_event_study()`. The function then resamples entire clusters, containing both treated and control units, with replacement, which allows for arbitrary correlation among units within the same cluster. Draws that end up with no treated or no control unit are discarded and counted in `n_boot_dropped`.

## Advanced Topics

### Time-Varying Covariates

SDID supports adjusting for time-varying confounders via the `covariates` argument. Following the "projected" approach of @clarke_synthetic_2024, the coefficients $\hat\beta$ are estimated by a two-way fixed effects regression of the outcome on the covariates over all untreated observations, and SDID is then applied to the residualized outcome $Y_{it} - X_{it}'\hat\beta$:

```r
# Example with time-varying covariates (e.g., retail price)
fit_cov <- scm_fit(
  cigsale ~ treated | state + year,
  data = smoking,
  method = "sdid",
  covariates = "retprice"
)
summary(fit_cov)
```

This example only illustrates the syntax. Covariates should not themselves be affected by the treatment, and the retail price is: Proposition 99 raised the cigarette tax, so adjusting for `retprice` absorbs part of the policy effect (the estimate shrinks to about $-2.3$ packs).

### Staggered Adoption

When different units receive treatment at different points in time, coresynth automatically detects the staggered timing and applies the cohort aggregation framework of @clarke_synthetic_2024: SDID is estimated separately for each adoption cohort $g$, and the cohort estimates are averaged with weights proportional to $N_{\text{tr},g} \times T_{\text{post},g}$:

```r
# Staggered adoption SDID fit
fit_stagg <- scm_fit(
  y ~ treated | unit + year,
  data = staggered_panel,
  method = "sdid",
  control_group = "never_treated" # Default in v1.0.0+
)
fit_stagg$cohort_estimates
```

In coresynth 1.0.0 and later, `control_group = "never_treated"` is the default, ensuring that only pure, never-treated units serve as donors for each adoption cohort to prevent contamination from future adopters.

## Tidy Ecosystem Integration & JSON Export

To ensure smooth integration into reproducible research pipelines, coresynth fully supports {broom} tidying methods and structured JSON serialization:

### Broom Integration: `tidy()` and `glance()`

```{r}
broom::tidy(inf_placebo)
```

```{r}
broom::glance(inf_placebo)
```

### Extracting Tidy Data via `plot_data()`

If you wish to create fully custom visualizations in ggplot2 or export tabular summaries, `plot_data()` provides raw data frames:

```{r}
# Extract aligned trend data
plot_data(core_sdid, type = "trend", align = TRUE) |> head()

# Extract unit and time weights
plot_data(core_sdid, type = "weights") |> head()
```

### Exporting Results to JSON

For cross-language pipelines (e.g., Python, dashboards) and archiving, use `export_json()`:

```r
export_json(core_sdid, file = "sdid_results.json", inference = inf_placebo)
```

## Summary & Feedback

Synthetic Difference-in-Differences is an estimator that addresses the weaknesses of both standard DID and classical SCM. With `{coresynth}`, running SDID is as simple as writing a standard regression formula, backed by fast C++ optimization, along with versatile tools for inference and visualization.

I hope coresynth helps accelerate your causal inference workflow.

If you have any questions, encounter bugs, or would like to request new features, please feel free to open an issue on the [GitHub Repository](https://github.com/yo5uke/coresynth/issues) or reach out on [X (\@5uke_y)](https://x.com/5uke_y)!
